Q131482.title: Hijrah
paras: The Hijrah ('migration') was the move of the Prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to the oasis town of Yathrib, afterwards known as Medina, in 622. On one side stood the small Muslim community of Mecca; on the other the leaders of Mecca's ruling Quraysh tribe, who opposed Muhammad's preaching. The people who received him in Medina were members of its two main Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj.

Muhammad began preaching in Mecca after the first revelations of around 610, denouncing the worship of idols and criticising the greed of rich merchants. As his following grew, Meccan leaders turned against him: his clan was boycotted and his followers persecuted. After the death, towards the end of the 610s, of his uncle Abu Talib, who had protected him, Muhammad looked for support outside the city. Men from Medina met him at al-Aqabah near Mecca and pledged themselves to him, the second time, at the pilgrimage of 622, promising to defend him as they would their own families. Muhammad then had his followers leave for Medina in small groups over about three months. When the Meccan leaders learned of the exodus they plotted to kill him; he slipped away with his companion Abu Bakr, hid for three days in a cave on Mount Thawr and then travelled to Medina by little-used paths. The day of his arrival is uncertain: HISTORY.com gives both 24 and 27 September 622, while Wikipedia notes that early historians disagreed on the exact day.
The migration was driven by the persecution in Mecca and by the invitation of the Medinans, whose Aws and Khazraj tribes had fought each other for many years and hoped that Muhammad could unite them.

In Medina Muhammad became the leader of an organised community; the agreement known as the Constitution of Medina made him the chief arbiter of disputes among its groups, including the Jewish tribes. From 623 he led raids on Meccan caravans, and within ten years of the Hijrah he was strong enough to return to Mecca and take the city. The Hijrah came to mark the beginning of Islamic history: in 638, the 17th year after it, the caliph Umar made the year of the Hijrah the first year of the Islamic calendar, whose first day corresponds to 16 July 622 in the Julian calendar.

Q134949.title: Winter War
Q134949.place: Finland (Karelian Isthmus, Ladoga Karelia, Kainuu, Lapland)
paras: The Winter War was fought between the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin and Finland, whose army was commanded by Marshal Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim. The Soviet Union invaded on 30 November 1939, three months after the start of the Second World War, and the war ended with the Moscow Peace Treaty in March 1940.

Stalin, free to act in the east after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact with Germany in August 1939, demanded that Finland give up border territory, including land on the Karelian Isthmus and islands, in exchange for land elsewhere, arguing that Leningrad, about 32 km from the border, needed protection. Finland refused. On 26 November 1939 Soviet reports claimed that a border post at Mainila had been shelled; historians later concluded that the shelling was a false-flag action by an NKVD unit on the Soviet side, and four days later the Red Army attacked. Most sources conclude that the Soviet Union meant to conquer all of Finland, pointing to the puppet Finnish communist government it set up, though some historians disagree.

The Red Army was far stronger, especially in tanks and aircraft, but its officer corps had been weakened by Stalin's purges, and it fared badly in temperatures as low as −43 °C against Finns who moved fast on skis. For more than two months the Finns held the Mannerheim Line on the Karelian Isthmus and inflicted heavy losses in battles at Taipale, Kollaa and the Raate Road. The League of Nations declared the attack illegal and expelled the Soviet Union. Britain and France planned to help Finland, but no help arrived. In February 1940, after reorganising and changing tactics, the Soviets broke through on the Karelian Isthmus, and Mannerheim urged peace while Finland could still bargain. The treaty was signed in Moscow late on 12 March, and the fighting ended on 13 March 1940.

Finland kept its independence but gave up about a tenth of its territory, including much of Karelia and the city of Viipuri (Vyborg); the share is given as 9 percent by Wikipedia, 10 percent by History UK and 11 percent by The Moscow Times. Some 422,000 to 450,000 Karelians, about 12 per cent of Finland's population, were evacuated from the ceded lands (History UK says around half a million). About 26,000 Finns were dead or missing, against roughly 127,000 to 168,000 Soviet soldiers. The Red Army's poor performance encouraged Hitler to believe that an invasion of the Soviet Union would succeed, and when Germany attacked in June 1941 Finland renewed the fight in the Continuation War.

Q154255.title: Munich Agreement
paras: The Munich Agreement was concluded in Munich in the night of 29–30 September 1938 by the leaders of four powers: Adolf Hitler for Germany, Neville Chamberlain for Britain, Édouard Daladier for France and Benito Mussolini for Italy. It handed Germany the Sudetenland, the border regions of Czechoslovakia where about three million people, mostly ethnic Germans, lived. Czechoslovakia itself was not a party to the talks, although its representatives were waiting in the town, and nor was the Soviet Union, an ally of France and Czechoslovakia.

From 17 September 1938 Germany waged a low-level undeclared war along the border. Chamberlain flew to meet Hitler twice, at Berchtesgaden and at Bad Godesberg, and on 20 September Britain and France formally asked Czechoslovakia to give up the Sudetenland; Poland and Hungary pressed claims of their own. At an emergency conference on 29–30 September the four powers quickly agreed on Hitler's terms. The text, dated 29 September in the Avalon Project's copy, set out that German troops would occupy four zones in stages from 1 October, that the evacuation would be completed by 10 October, and that an international commission would draw the final frontier and decide where plebiscites should be held. On 30 September President Edvard Beneš gave in to the combined pressure and accepted the terms.

Britain and France hoped to avoid a major war by giving way to Hitler, a policy of appeasement; Hitler declared that the Sudetenland was his last territorial demand in Europe. Much of Europe welcomed the agreement, and Chamberlain, back in London on 30 September, spoke of 'peace for our time'. Others saw it differently: Winston Churchill told the House of Commons on 5 October that Britain had 'sustained a total and unmitigated defeat'. In Czech and Slovak it is still called the 'Munich Betrayal', because France had been bound to Czechoslovakia by an alliance of 1924 and a military pact of 1925. Today the agreement is generally regarded as a failed act of appeasement.

Czechoslovakia lost its mountain frontier and border fortifications. In November 1938 the First Vienna Award gave southern Slovakia and Subcarpathian Ruthenia's southern part to Hungary, and Poland took further small areas. In March 1939 Slovakia declared independence under German protection and Hitler, breaking his promise, occupied the rest of the Czech lands as the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, taking over the Czechoslovak army's weapons and the country's arms industry.

Q15860072.title: Russo-Ukrainian war
Q15860072.place: Ukraine (Crimea and the Donbas, then much of the country)
paras: The Russo-Ukrainian war is fought between Ukraine and Russia, together with the armed groups Russia backed in eastern Ukraine. It began in February 2014 and, in its first eight years, centred on Crimea and the Donbas region of the south-east; in February 2022 Russia widened it into a full-scale invasion, and it was still going on in late 2026.

In late 2013 Ukraine's president Viktor Yanukovych, under pressure from Moscow, dropped plans for a closer economic agreement with the European Union. The decision set off the Euromaidan protests, and in February 2014 Yanukovych fled. Unmarked Russian troops then occupied Crimea; after a referendum held under occupation on 16 March, Russia annexed the peninsula on 18 March 2014, the first annexation of one European country's territory by another since the Second World War. In April Russian-backed militants seized towns in the Donbas and proclaimed the Donetsk and Luhansk 'People's Republics', and Russia supported them covertly with its own troops, tanks and artillery. The Minsk Protocol of September 2014 and the Minsk II agreements of February 2015 did not end the fighting; the front froze into trench warfare with frequent ceasefire breaches.

Behind the war lay a long contest over Ukraine's direction since independence in 1991: a largely Ukrainian-speaking west favoured ties with Europe, much of the Russian-speaking east closer ties with Russia, and Moscow sought to keep its influence in Ukraine, all the more after the Orange Revolution of 2004. Vladimir Putin presented the fall of Yanukovych as a Western-backed coup threatening Russians in Crimea, a claim Western leaders rejected as propaganda.

The Council on Foreign Relations counts more than fourteen thousand people killed in the Donbas between 2014 and 2021. Ukraine, officially neutral when the war began, revived plans to join NATO. After a large Russian build-up around Ukraine's borders in 2021, Russia recognised the two separatist republics in early 2022 and on 24 February launched the full-scale invasion, turning the conflict into the largest war in Europe since 1945 and causing hundreds of thousands of deaths and a refugee crisis.

Q178810.title: Syrian Civil War
paras: The Syrian Civil War lasted from March 2011 to December 2024. On one side stood the government of President Bashar al-Assad, backed by Russia, Iran and Shia militias armed by Iran, above all Lebanon's Hezbollah. Against it fought a fragmented opposition: the Free Syrian Army, formed by army defectors in July 2011, and a growing number of Islamist brigades, supported to varying degrees by Turkey, Western powers and Gulf Arab states. Jihadist groups, al-Qaeda's Syrian branch Jabhat al-Nusra and the Islamic State, pursued their own aims, while Kurdish-led forces, later the Syrian Democratic Forces, fought the Islamic State with the help of a US-led coalition.

In March 2011, as uprisings spread across the Arab world, teenagers in the southern city of Deraa wrote 'The people want the fall of the regime' on a school wall and were arrested and tortured. Protests followed and spread to Damascus, Homs and Hama; the government answered with shooting, mass arrests and, from late April, a siege of Deraa by tanks, and some opponents took up arms. Jabhat al-Nusra announced itself in January 2012, and in 2013 the Islamic State seized territory across eastern Syria and western Iraq. In 2013 a chemical attack in Ghouta, near Damascus, was the deadliest use of chemical weapons since the Iran–Iraq War. From 2014 a US-led coalition struck the Islamic State, and in September 2015 Russia's air force entered the war, helping Assad regain the upper hand; government forces retook eastern Aleppo in December 2016 after a long siege, and the rebels were pushed back mainly to Idlib in the north-west. In late 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) launched a rapid offensive, took the main cities in days, and on 8 December 2024 Assad fled to Moscow as rebels entered Damascus.

The uprising grew out of four decades of autocratic rule by the Assad family, which had brutally crushed a revolt in Hama in 1982, together with corruption, unemployment and lack of political freedom, made worse by economic reforms that favoured regime insiders and by a record drought from 2006 to 2010. Assad met the protests with force rather than reform, and outside powers then turned the war into a contest between themselves. The regime's final collapse came when its allies were weakened: Hezbollah by Israel's campaign in Lebanon in 2024, Iran by Israeli strikes, and Russia by its war in Ukraine.

The toll is disputed. The UN Human Rights Office estimated that 306,887 civilians were killed between March 2011 and March 2021; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights had documented 503,064 deaths by March 2023 and estimated more than 613,400 (both as reported by the BBC). Nearly fourteen million people, more than half of the pre-war population, were driven from their homes, many of them as refugees to Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan. After Assad's fall a transitional government was formed and HTS's former leader Ahmed al-Sharaa became president, but clashes in parts of the country continued.

Q182524.title: Vostok 1: the first human spaceflight
Q182524.place: Baikonur, Kazakh SSR, Soviet Union, and Earth orbit
paras: On 12 April 1961 the Soviet Union launched Vostok 1, the first spaceflight to carry a human being. Its pilot was Yuri Gagarin, a young Soviet air force officer who had been chosen in 1960, with about twenty others, for cosmonaut training; Gherman Titov and Grigori Nelyubov were his backups. The flight was part of the space race between the Soviet Union and the United States, whose Project Mercury was preparing its own first crewed flights.

Vostok 1 lifted off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome at 9:07 a.m. Moscow time on a rocket adapted from the R-7, the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile, which had launched Sputnik in 1957. The spherical Vostok 3KA capsule made a single orbit of the Earth at a height of between about 181 and 327 km. On the way down Gagarin ejected from the capsule at about 7,000 m and landed separately by parachute, as the design required; early Soviet reports left this detail out. He came down in the Saratov region, south-west of the town of Engels. The flight took 108 minutes; NASA's StarChild page describes this as time in orbit, the other sources as the time from launch to landing.

The Soviet programme had been pursued in secret, and a series of uncrewed test flights between May 1960 and March 1961, the last two fully successful, cleared the way for a crewed launch. Both Cold War superpowers wanted to develop spaceflight quickly, and above all to be first to launch a human successfully.

Gagarin became an international hero. Less than a month later, on 5 May 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space with a 15-minute suborbital flight, and John Glenn made the first American orbital flight on 20 February 1962.

Q201684.title: Wall Street crash of 1929
Q201684.place: New York Stock Exchange, New York City, United States
paras: The Wall Street crash of 1929 was the collapse of share prices on the New York Stock Exchange in the last week of October 1929. Those involved were the millions of American investors, many of them ordinary men and women, the brokers and banks who had lent them money to buy shares, and the Federal Reserve, which had tried to curb the speculation.

Share prices had soared through the 1920s: the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about six-fold from 63 in August 1921 to a peak of 381 on 3 September 1929. After a nervous September the market broke on Thursday 24 October, 'Black Thursday', when a record 12.9 million shares changed hands; leading bankers bought large blocks of shares above market prices to restore confidence, but the effort failed. On 'Black Monday', 28 October, the Dow fell nearly 13 percent, and on 'Black Tuesday', 29 October, it dropped nearly 12 percent more as some 16 million shares were traded. By mid-November the Dow had lost almost half its value. The New York Federal Reserve Bank bought government securities, lent freely and cut its discount rate, so that the commercial banks at the centre of the storm stayed open.

The boom had been fed by easy credit: buyers typically put down about 10 percent of a share's price and borrowed the rest, using the shares as collateral, so falling prices forced sales that drove prices lower still. The Federal Reserve, worried that speculation was draining credit from industry and trade, raised the New York discount rate to 6 percent in August 1929; under the gold standard this pushed other countries to raise their rates and helped slow economies around the world.

The crash wiped out the savings of many investors and frightened consumers into cutting spending on goods such as cars, so firms cut production and unemployment rose. The decline went on until July 1932, when the Dow closed at 41.22, 89 percent below its peak; it did not regain its 1929 level until November 1954. The crash marked the start of the Great Depression, though economists debate how far it caused it: the Federal Reserve's historians argue that its effects alone might have faded and that the banking panics of 1930 to 1933 turned a sharp recession into the longest and deepest depression in American history.

Q21479779.title: November 2015 Paris attacks
paras: On the evening of Friday 13 November 2015 a team of ten Islamic State militants, organised from a terrorist cell based in Brussels, attacked Paris and its northern suburb of Saint-Denis. Most of the attackers had been born and raised in France or Belgium. The Islamic State group claimed the attacks, which are considered the deadliest in peacetime French history.

From 21:16, three suicide bombers blew themselves up outside the Stade de France in Saint-Denis during an international football match, having failed to get into the stadium. A second group fired on crowded cafés and restaurants in central Paris, and one of them detonated his explosive vest. A third group opened fire at an Eagles of Death Metal concert attended by about 1,500 people at the Bataclan theatre and took hostages; when police stormed the building the attackers were shot or set off their vests. In all 130 people were killed, 90 of them at the Bataclan, and 416 were physically injured. On 18 November the suspected ringleader, Abdelhamid Abaaoud, was killed in a police raid in Saint-Denis. Accounts of the attackers' fate differ slightly: Wikipedia says seven died at the scenes and two in the Saint-Denis raid, while the Associated Press, as published by NPR, says the nine others all died that night. The tenth, Salah Abdeslam, who had driven the stadium bombers, escaped.

The attackers were motivated by Islamist extremism, and their stated aim was retaliation for French air strikes on the Islamic State in Syria and Iraq; France had been on high alert since the Charlie Hebdo shooting and related attacks in January 2015.

France declared a state of emergency, which lasted until 2017, when many of its measures were written into ordinary law; armed patrols became a permanent sight in public places. On 15 November France carried out its biggest air strike yet against the Islamic State. After a nine-month trial, a special terrorism court on 29 June 2022 convicted Abdeslam, the only surviving attacker, of murder and sentenced him to life without parole, France's most severe sentence; nineteen other men were convicted of helping the attackers.

Q21707860.title: Paris Agreement
paras: The Paris Agreement is a treaty on climate change adopted on 12 December 2015 at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP21) held at Le Bourget near Paris, under the French presidency of Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius. Unlike the Kyoto Protocol, which bound only developed countries, it asks every country to commit to cutting its emissions; almost all the world's states have joined it.

The agreement was negotiated by the parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change between 30 November and 12 December 2015, after the Copenhagen conference of 2009 had failed to produce a binding successor to Kyoto. It was opened for signature on 22 April 2016 and entered into force on 4 November 2016. Its goal is to hold the rise in global average temperature to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Each country sets its own targets, its 'nationally determined contribution', and is expected to submit a new, stronger one every five years; richer countries are to help poorer ones with finance, and progress is reviewed in a 'global stocktake', the first of which ended at COP28 in 2023. The detailed rules were agreed at Katowice in 2018 and completed at Glasgow in 2021.

Behind the agreement lay the scientific warnings that warming beyond these limits would bring far greater risks, and the lesson of Kyoto, which had left out the developing countries that had become major emitters. A system of national pledges, set from the bottom up, made it possible for all to take part.

The agreement is legally binding, but the national targets themselves are not; only the duty to prepare and report them is. The United States, the second-largest emitter, is the only country to have left it: President Donald Trump announced its withdrawal in 2017, which took effect in 2020; President Joe Biden rejoined in 2021; and Trump withdrew again at the start of his second term in January 2025, with effect from 2026. Global temperatures kept rising: the World Meteorological Organization reported that 2024 was about 1.55 °C above pre-industrial levels, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

Q36204.title: 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami
paras: At 14:46 local time on 11 March 2011 an undersea megathrust earthquake struck about 72 km east of the Oshika Peninsula in the Tōhoku region of north-eastern Honshu, Japan. Its magnitude is given as 9.0–9.1 by Wikipedia and 9.1 by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA): the largest ever recorded in Japan and, according to NOAA, the third-largest in the world since 1900. The disaster is known in Japan as the Great East Japan Earthquake.

The shaking lasted about six minutes. Within 30 minutes a tsunami reached the coast, overtopping sea walls along some 2,000 km of Japan's Pacific shore; waves reached about 40 m (40.5 m at Miyako in Iwate Prefecture, according to Wikipedia). Whole towns were swept away: more than 123,000 houses were completely destroyed and almost a million damaged, and NOAA attributes 98 percent of the damage to the tsunami. At the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant the tsunami knocked out the power supply and cooling, and the cores of three reactors largely melted down in the first three days, releasing radioactivity and forcing the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of residents from the surrounding zones.

The earthquake was caused by thrust faulting on the boundary where the Pacific plate slides beneath the plate carrying northern Japan, a zone that had produced deadly tsunamis before, in 1611, 1896 and 1933. The quake moved Honshu about 2.4 metres to the east and shifted the Earth's axis by an estimated 10 to 25 cm.

The tolls differ by source. Japan's National Police Agency counted 15,901 deaths and 2,519 people missing as of March 2026 (as reported by NOAA), while Wikipedia gives official figures released in 2021 of 19,759 deaths and 2,553 missing. NOAA puts the cost in Japan at 220 billion US dollars, Wikipedia at over 300 billion; either way it was the costliest natural disaster in history. The tsunami was measured across the Pacific, killing one person in Indonesia and one in California, where warning systems helped limit the loss of life. Four years later, in 2015, almost 229,000 people were still living away from their homes.

Q46362.title: Congress of Vienna
paras: The Congress of Vienna met from September 1814 to June 1815 to settle Europe after the defeat of Napoleon. It was chaired by the Austrian foreign minister Prince Klemens von Metternich. The leading parts were played by the four victorious allies, represented by Metternich for Austria, Viscount Castlereagh for Britain, Tsar Alexander I for Russia and Prince Karl August von Hardenberg for Prussia, and by defeated France, represented by Talleyrand; monarchs and envoys from across Europe came to press their own claims.

The four allies first meant to decide everything themselves, but Talleyrand and the Spanish envoy Pedro Gómez Labrador protested, and France was admitted to the inner circle of great powers. The hardest dispute was the Polish-Saxon question: Russia wanted most of the Duchy of Warsaw and Prussia all of Saxony, whose king had sided with Napoleon, while Austria, Britain and France resisted. A compromise was reached by early 1815: Russia received most of Poland as a kingdom under the tsar, and Prussia a large part of Saxony (60 percent according to Wikipedia, a third according to the Encyclopedia of Modern Europe) and new lands on the Rhine. The congress was nearly finished when Napoleon escaped from Elba in March 1815; the Final Act, which gathered all the separate treaties, was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before his final defeat at Waterloo.

The peacemakers wanted a lasting balance of power in which no state, France above all, could dominate Europe again, and the conservative monarchies also wanted to hold back revolutionary and liberal movements. To contain France, Belgium was joined to an enlarged Kingdom of the Netherlands; Austria took Lombardy–Venetia in northern Italy, and Habsburg relatives were placed in Modena, Parma and Tuscany. A German Confederation of the German states was created, with Austria presiding. The congress also guaranteed Swiss neutrality, condemned the slave trade and declared freedom of navigation on rivers such as the Rhine and the Danube.

The settlement gave rise to the Concert of Europe, under which the great powers met to keep the peace, and it shaped Europe's political order for decades without a general war. Historians judge it differently: some credit it with a long peace, others blame it for suppressing national, democratic and liberal movements in the interest of the old monarchies. Sources also disagree on the signatories: Wikipedia says Spain refused to sign in 1815, in protest at the Italian settlement among other reasons, and signed only in 1817, while UNESCO's description of the Austrian copy and the Encyclopedia of Modern Europe list Spain among the eight signing powers.

Q47359.title: Kyoto Protocol
paras: The Kyoto Protocol was an international treaty adopted in Kyoto, Japan, on 11 December 1997 by the parties to the 1992 United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It was the first legally binding climate treaty: it set binding limits on greenhouse gas emissions for developed countries, while developing countries, including major emitters such as China and India, had no obligation to cut theirs.

The protocol covered carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and other greenhouse gases. Developed countries were to reduce emissions by an average of about 5 percent below 1990 levels, in the Council on Foreign Relations' summary, each with its own target; they could also meet part of their targets through 'flexibility mechanisms': emissions trading, joint implementation and the clean development mechanism, which earned credits for projects that cut emissions in other countries. The treaty needed ratification by at least 55 states; it came into force on 16 February 2005, after Russia and Canada had ratified it in 2004. The United States signed it in 1998 under President Clinton but never ratified it: the Senate had already voted in 1997, in the non-binding Byrd–Hagel resolution, against any agreement of that kind, and the US later withdrew its signature.

The treaty rested on the scientific consensus that the world is warming and that human emissions of carbon dioxide are driving it, and on the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities': developed countries, historically responsible for most of the gases already in the atmosphere, should act first.

In the first commitment period, 2008 to 2012, all 36 fully participating countries met their targets, helped by the 2008 financial crisis and by the collapse of industry in the former Eastern Bloc after 1990; yet global emissions rose by 32 percent from 1990 to 2010. Canada withdrew with effect from December 2012. The Doha Amendment extended the protocol to 2020 with binding targets for 37 countries, and the Paris Agreement of 2015, which requires pledges from all countries, took its place.

Q48249.title: Falklands War
Q48249.place: Falkland Islands and South Georgia, South Atlantic
paras: The Falklands War of April to June 1982 was fought between Argentina, ruled by a military junta under General Leopoldo Galtieri, and the United Kingdom under Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, over the Falkland Islands, a small British overseas territory about 300 miles (almost 500 km) off Argentina's coast, and its dependencies of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

On 2 April 1982 Argentine forces seized the islands in a surprise invasion. Britain assembled a task force of about 100 ships, whose first elements sailed on 5 April for the South Atlantic, some 8,000 miles from home. Special forces and Royal Marines recaptured South Georgia between 21 and 25 April. On 2 May the British submarine HMS Conqueror's torpedoes sank the Argentine cruiser General Belgrano, killing 321 of her crew and two civilians, and Argentine air attacks sank several British ships, among them the Atlantic Conveyor, hit by an Exocet missile on 25 May with the loss of most of the heavy-lift helicopters. British troops landed at San Carlos Water on East Falkland on 21 May, won the first major land battle at Goose Green on 28 May and, after night battles for the mountains around Stanley, received the surrender of the Argentine commander, Mario Menéndez, on 14 June 1982.

The war grew out of a long dispute over sovereignty. Argentina claims the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, as its own and called its action the recovery of its territory; Britain regarded the islands as a Crown colony since 1841, and the islanders, mostly descended from British settlers, strongly wanted to remain British. Years of talks, urged by the United Nations since 1965, had not settled the question, and the junta hoped to bring the islands under Buenos Aires at last.

In the 74 days of fighting, 649 Argentine servicemen, 255 British servicemen and three Falkland Islanders were killed. In Argentina the defeat set off large protests against the military government, hastening its fall and the return of democracy; in Britain Thatcher's government gained in popularity and was re-elected with a larger majority in 1983. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were restored in 1989, but Argentina still claims the islands.

Q79911.title: Russian Civil War
paras: The Russian Civil War was fought across the former Russian Empire after the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin seized power in the October Revolution of 1917. On one side stood the Bolsheviks' Red Army; on the other the Whites, led mainly by former imperial officers such as Alexander Kolchak in Siberia, Anton Denikin and later Pyotr Wrangel in the south and Nikolai Yudenich in the north-west. Anarchists such as Nestor Makhno's army in Ukraine, Left Socialist-Revolutionaries, peasant 'green armies' and national independence movements fought as well, and foreign states intervened, most of them against the Reds.

Resistance to the Bolsheviks grew into full-scale war in May–June 1918, when the Czechoslovak Legion, formed from captured Austro-Hungarian soldiers, revolted in Siberia; the Allies then landed forces in northern Russia and Siberia, hoping to restore the Eastern Front against Germany, which Russia had left by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. Leon Trotsky reorganised the Red Guards into the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army. In November 1918 Kolchak was named 'Supreme Ruler' of the anti-Bolshevik government at Omsk. In 1919 the Whites attacked from the east in March, the south in July and the west in October, but each offensive was beaten back, and by early 1920 they had been defeated on all three fronts; Kolchak was handed over by the Czechoslovaks and executed. The remnants of Denikin's armies under Wrangel were evacuated from Crimea in November 1920. Sporadic fighting went on in the Far East until the capture of Vladivostok in October 1922.

The war arose because the seizure of power by one party was not accepted by many groups: landowners and factory owners who lost their property, officers, liberals and other socialists, and many opponents of the harsh Brest-Litovsk peace, which cost Russia about a third of its population and a third of its factories. The Whites never united politically or co-ordinated their armies, while the Bolsheviks held the industrial heartland, had more men and a single ideology.

The Bolshevik victory produced the Russian Soviet republic and later the Soviet Union, though Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland kept their independence and the Peace of Riga of March 1921 divided Ukraine and Belarus with Poland. The human cost was enormous: Wikipedia gives an estimated 7 to 12 million casualties, mostly civilians, while David Bullock, author of The Russian Civil War (2008), as quoted by Spartacus Educational, put the deaths at 7 to 14 million, including about 5 million in the famines of 1921–22 caused by the war's economic disruption. Sources also differ on the end date: 1920, 1921 or October 1922.

Q81068910.title: COVID-19 pandemic
paras: The COVID-19 pandemic was the worldwide spread of a new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, and of the disease it causes, COVID-19. The first known cases were in Wuhan, in Hubei province, China, in late 2019; molecular-clock studies place the first infections between October and November 2019, and many early patients were linked to the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market, which also sold live animals. On 31 December 2019 the Wuhan Municipal Health Commission reported a cluster of pneumonia cases, and this is the date the World Health Organization (WHO) gives for first learning of the virus.

The genetic sequence of the virus was shared publicly in January 2020 (on 10 January according to Wikipedia, on 12 January according to WHO's timeline), and WHO's timeline records the first confirmed case outside China, in Thailand, on 13 January. A WHO mission reported evidence of human-to-human transmission in Wuhan on 22 January. On 30 January WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern, when 7,818 cases had been confirmed, 82 of them in 18 countries outside China, and on 11 March 2020 it described the outbreak as a pandemic. Governments answered with travel restrictions, lockdowns, closures of businesses, mask mandates, quarantines, testing and contact tracing. Vaccines, developed at unusual speed, were given to the public from December 2020, while new variants such as Delta and Omicron spread in waves.

The scientific consensus is that the virus most likely passed to humans from bats or a closely related mammal; the alternative that it escaped from a laboratory has been proposed but is not the majority view. It spread easily between people, and Wuhan, a transport hub, was busy with travel around the Chinese New Year.

More than seven million deaths were officially attributed to COVID-19 (7,116,673 by 6 September 2026, according to Wikipedia's figures), but deaths above the normal level were far higher: WHO estimated 14.9 million excess deaths by the end of 2021, against 5.4 million reported. The pandemic caused the deepest global recession since the Great Depression and widespread supply shortages. After 13.3 billion vaccine doses had been given, WHO declared on 5 May 2023 that COVID-19 was an established, ongoing health issue and no longer a public health emergency of international concern.

Q93304.title: Code of Hammurabi
paras: The Code of Hammurabi is a collection of laws issued in the name of Hammurabi, the sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, who ruled from about 1792 to about 1750 BC. It was composed around 1753 BC, near the end of a reign in which Hammurabi had made Babylon the dominant power of the Mesopotamian plain by war and diplomacy, at times turning on former allies such as Eshnunna, Elam and Mari.

The best-known copy is a basalt stele 2.25 m tall. At the top a relief shows Hammurabi before Shamash, the sun god and god of justice, who sits on a throne; below, about 4,130 lines of cuneiform text in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian set out a poetic prologue and epilogue and, in between, some 282 laws. The laws are written as cases, 'if ... then', and cover crimes, family life, property, trade, wages and slaves. Many punishments follow the principle of retaliation: law 196 orders that a man who puts out another man's eye shall lose his own eye, and the penalty often depended on the social class of the victim.

In the prologue Hammurabi says the gods gave him his rule so that the strong should not oppress the weak, and the relief presents his justice as sanctioned by Shamash. Scholars still debate what the text was for: whether it was legislation actually applied in court, a record of the king's decisions, or a work of jurisprudence and royal self-presentation.

Scribes copied and studied the text for more than a thousand years. About six centuries after it was made, the stele was carried off as plunder, probably from Sippar, to the Elamite city of Susa in present-day Iran, where a French archaeological mission led by Jacques de Morgan found it in 1901–1902. It is now in the Louvre in Paris. Since then it has become one of the most famous legal texts of the ancient world, discussed for its links with the Mosaic law of the Bible, and replicas stand in institutions such as the headquarters of the United Nations.

Law 196: if a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out; lex talionis; penalties varied by class (awīlum, muškēnum, slave).
Prologue: rule granted by the gods so that the strong should not harm/oppress the weak; the relief legitimises the king's sovereignty and justice.
The purpose is debated: legislation, law report or jurisprudence.
The text was copied by scribes for over a millennium; the stele was taken as plunder about 600 years after its creation, probably from Sippar (Roth), to Susa.
Found at Susa in 1901 (Wikipedia) / 1901–1902 (Louvre) by the mission of Jacques de Morgan; now in the Louvre.
Discussion of its influence on the Mosaic Law; replicas including at UN headquarters.

Q944.title: Quantum mechanics
Q944.place: Europe (Berlin, Copenhagen, Göttingen, Zurich and elsewhere)
paras: Quantum mechanics, the physics of atoms and their parts, grew out of the work of many physicists over about three decades, mostly in Germany, Denmark, Austria, Switzerland, France and Britain: Max Planck, Albert Einstein, Niels Bohr, Louis de Broglie, Werner Heisenberg, Max Born, Pascual Jordan, Erwin Schrödinger and Paul Dirac among them. Its starting point, the year the map uses, is 1900, when Planck in Berlin found a formula for the radiation given off by a heated 'black body'.

Classical physics predicted that a hot body should give off unlimited energy at short wavelengths, an obviously wrong result later called the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck solved the problem in 1900 by assuming that radiation comes in 'quanta' whose energy is set by a new constant, now called Planck's constant. In 1905 Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by treating light itself as made of quanta, and in 1913 Bohr built a quantum model of the hydrogen atom that accounted for its spectral lines. In his doctoral thesis of 1924 de Broglie proposed that matter, too, has wave properties.

These piecemeal ideas, the 'old quantum theory', were replaced by a full theory in 1925 to 1927. Heisenberg wrote his first paper on quantum mechanics in 1925, which he, Born and Jordan developed into matrix mechanics; in 1926 Schrödinger published his wave equation, and he later showed that the two approaches were equivalent. Born concluded that the theory gives only probabilities for the outcome of an individual event, and in 1927 Heisenberg stated the uncertainty principle: measuring a particle's position disturbs its momentum. From about 1927 Dirac worked to unify the approaches and bring quantum theory into line with special relativity.

The theory was the answer to experiments that classical mechanics could not explain: black-body radiation, the photoelectric effect and the spectra of atoms. Planck received the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1918 for his discovery of energy quanta, and Heisenberg the prize for 1932 for the creation of quantum mechanics. The theory went on to explain chemical bonding and, through Dirac's work, led towards quantum electrodynamics. What it says about reality is still disputed: physicists and philosophers continue to argue over the 'measurement problem' and offer competing interpretations, including the Copenhagen, Everettian and Bohmian ones.
